title: Sojourner Truth
hookLine: a freed woman preacher who spoke for abolition and women's rights

cards: A courtroom in New York. A tall Black woman, once enslaved, stands before the judge. Her young son has been sold away, illegally, to a planter in the South, and she wants him back.
Nobody expects her to win. She can't read. She has no money.
Her first language isn't even English. She speaks anyway, and keeps speaking, and she gets her son back. Her name then was Isabella.
Later she chose a new one. A sojourner is someone who travels and doesn't settle, and truth was what she meant to carry. Today: Sojourner Truth.

teach.b: Isabella was born into slavery in New York, in a household where she grew up speaking Dutch. When freedom was slow in coming, she walked away from her enslaver with her baby daughter in her arms. Not ran, she said later.

Walked. Around then her faith became fierce and personal. In the account of her life she dictated, she describes an overwhelming awareness of God, and then of Jesus standing between her and God, a friend.

Years later she said the Spirit was calling her to travel, so she took her new name and went: preaching at camp meetings, singing, speaking against slavery, and, just as boldly, for the rights of women.
One speech of hers, at a women's rights meeting in Ohio, is still quoted. The honest part: she didn't write it down. Others did, and the versions differ a lot.
The well-known refrain people quote comes from one later version. But one thread runs through the reports. Men had argued against women's rights from the Bible, and she answered from the Bible too.
In at least one version she asks where Christ came from, and answers: from God and a woman. Scripture had room for her.
The prophet Joel said, in the King James Bible: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy."
Paul wrote, "there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." Some women preachers of her day pointed to lines like these.
She stood up in rooms where nobody wanted to hear a woman, a Black woman, a formerly enslaved woman, say anything at all. She said it anyway.

how: Some churches remember Sojourner Truth as a preacher and reformer, and her story is told in sermons and classes on faith, freedom and women's voices.

games.q: you're at a women's rights meeting. men stand up and argue from the Bible that women should stay quiet. what do you do?
o: stay silent, since it's their scripture to quote.
answer them from the Bible yourself.
games.why: she stood and answered from scripture, and in at least one version asked where Christ came from: from God and a woman.

practice: Bring to mind the next room where your view will be asked for, or not: a work call, a family dinner, a meeting. Find the true sentence you keep swallowing, and say it once, silently and plainly, without apology.
If you pray, ask for courage; if you don't, simply hold the sentence steady.

wordCard.voice: Sojourner Truth. A name she chose: a traveler, carrying truth, who preached against slavery and for the rights of women.

orig.note: Greek: a sojourning, a stay as a stranger far from home — the word in 1 Peter 1:17 for the time of your sojourning.

carryVoice: Your line: a woman speaks. Even where nobody wanted to listen. That's nine hundred nineteen days.
